title: What if…
lede: Three decisions where the story could have gone differently. The “What if” panels are speculation, labeled as such.

forks.actual: On March 13, 2003 Metromedia announced an agreement to sell Steak and Ale, then 66 restaurants, with Ponderosa and Bonanza to APEX, a Dallas restaurant group, subject to financing. Six months later the deal had become a management arrangement covering all four chains, and Steak and Ale stayed inside S&A Restaurant Corp.[^23][^24]
forks.whatif: Under separate ownership Steak and Ale would not have been one of the 38 debtors of July 2008. That is all that can be said with confidence. APEX managed small regional concepts, the sale depended on financing that evidently did not arrive, and a 66-restaurant steakhouse chain would still have met Outback, LongHorn and the 2008 recession on its own.

forks.actual: Bennigan’s was franchised at home and abroad; in 2008 it had 96 franchised restaurants in the United States alone. Metromedia’s franchise page offered Bennigan’s, Bonanza and Ponderosa. The 58 Steak and Ale restaurants of May 2008 were all company-owned, and all closed.[^4][^8][^24]
forks.whatif: Even a few dozen franchised steakhouses would probably have stayed open on July 29, as the franchised Bennigan’s did, and kept the brand trading while it changed hands. The counter-argument is the cost: a dinner house of about 10,000 square feet is a harder thing to sell to a franchisee than a bar and grill, and the new owners spent years after 2015 looking for one.[^32]

forks.actual: The owners filed for liquidation, not reorganisation, weeks after saying they were preparing a proposal for their lenders. Three months later Metromedia’s other restaurant company, with Ponderosa and Bonanza, filed under Chapter 11 and tried to reorganise.[^8][^9][^13]
forks.whatif: A Chapter 11 case might have kept the better Steak and Ale restaurants open under court protection while a buyer was found, as happened to the sibling steakhouses. It needs a lender willing to finance it, and in the summer of 2008 an analyst told the Times that banks had become less willing to lend to restaurants.[^3] The choice of Chapter 7 suggests the owners or the lenders saw nothing worth financing.
